discussionThreads.author: anlthms
discussionThreads.reason: New competitor claim with essential caveat preserved; current replies verified in logged-out Newest view. Recipe still unresolved.
discussionThreads.summary: mikelou1 reports an 87% local Qwen run under time constraints at roughly four-L4 speed (October 20 03:00 UTC). At 06:26 UTC the same author explicitly says 87% likely will not transfer, would be surprised by even 80%, and hopes for roughly 75%; those are expectations, not a submitted result. A later reply at 08:54 UTC says they are not very concerned about overfit because they get few runs. Other participants discuss throughput and the local-to-leaderboard gap. No complete recipe or independently verified new leaderboard score was supplied.
discussionThreads.title: Qwen3.8 or something else?

discussionThreads.summary: Kaggle Staff member Dustin says dataset download time does not count toward submission runtime. He explains that the live interactive quota display is an estimate and final usage corrects to container runtime when the session stops; data added while a container is running consumes quota. The staff explanation is publicly readable. Expanded CPMP acknowledgment says he had not checked the final adjustment and assumes staff is right; this is not independent confirmation.

discussionThreads.author: dmitriigluzdov
discussionThreads.reason: Earlier lead re-read without login; body and visible replies publicly accessible. Preserve attribution and distinguish participant results from predictions.
discussionThreads.summary: Dmitrii Gluzdov reports synthetic ARC-rule fine-tuning improves performance on unseen generated rules but has not shown a leaderboard gain. The current post describes 1,369 executable rules and 41,070 generated puzzles, two training approaches, and reported public scores of 30.83 for base NVARC, 29.03 for early LoRA, 27.92 for full LoRA and 29.17 for added blocks. He reports rerun variation of roughly two to four points. Training only on the hard-example file remains untried. These are the author’s experiments and noise estimate; augmented examples are not independent puzzles.
discussionThreads.title: Tried fine-tuning NVARC on new synthetic ARC tasks

socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize reports verified Reflection Beam 1.0 scores: ARC-AGI-2 23.5% at $0.61/task and ARC-AGI-1 74.0% at $0.31/task. Best scores use xhigh reasoning; high reaches 20.0% on ARC-AGI-2 at about 43% lower cost.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: New official model evaluation. Linked result page independently read in Chrome: semi-private best scores match. This is benchmark evaluation, not a Kaggle team score.

socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize places Argon behind Astra’s 99.9% ARC-AGI-3 result. It reports 62% fewer actions than the human baseline on the 25 public games, matching or beating three speedrun records and coming within 10% on six others.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Keep the public-demo action comparison separate from the semi-private Verified score.

socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize says API issues prevented complete standard-harness testing: low reasoning completed 42/55 games for 49.8%; medium completed 46/55 for 46.3%; high completed 19/55 and no score was published. Reported scores retain partial credit across all 55 games. Provider adapter preserves opaque reasoning and permits automatic compaction; standard harness carries notes between turns. Costs use introductory $2 input/$10 output per million tokens.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Material limit on harness comparisons. Do not present incomplete standard-harness runs as a clean capability ceiling.

socialPosts.author: arcprize
socialPosts.summary: ARC Prize announces Gemini 4 Argon Verified results: ARC-AGI-3 97.5% at $4.8K with the provider adapter and 49.8% at $5.8K with the standard harness; ARC-AGI-2 91.3% at $0.32/task and ARC-AGI-1 98.5% at $0.16/task. It calls Google DeepMind the second frontier lab above 95% on ARC-AGI-3.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Consequential organizer result. Separate from Kaggle standings. Standard-harness API incompletion is essential context; primary results introduction says 91.2% on v2 while its table and announcement say 91.3%.

socialPosts.author: gklambauer
socialPosts.summary: Klambauer announces KronLSTM and links the new Kronecker Delta Rule paper. The authors propose a targeted association update for recurrent linear attention, report competitive long-context performance, and link open-source code and models. No ARC score is reported.
socialPosts.whyItMatters: Research lead discovered in fses91’s separate Reposts feed. The primary arXiv abstract was checked independently; architecture claims remain attributed, and no Kaggle roster identity is inferred.

discussionThreads.reason: New substantive participant experiments and negative results; signed-in body/reply read, then verified readable without login.
discussionThreads.summary: Francise Liang reports stopping work and shares tests of Franzen’s public Milestone 2 notebook on an RTX Pro 6000, with 25 public games and two passes per run. Two unchanged runs averaged 47.30 and 48.92; per-game differences had a reported standard deviation of 24 points. Increasing concurrent streams from ten to fourteen reduced the reported mean from 47.30 to 29.90 and throughput; stopping stalled levels at 110k tokens gave 38.97 versus a two-run baseline average of 48.11. Liang recommends repeated comparisons. These are participant measurements on public games, not independently reproduced results or hidden-board scores. Reply author xiaoz259 attributes poor throughput to insufficient KV-cache memory and lane preemption.

sections.heading: Two racks behind a double stronghold
sections.text:
Tufa Labs holds first place on both ARC public boards — and has now announced two NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks running in Stockholm. Its October 19 message makes the purpose plain: more computing capacity for more experiments at scale. DELTA handled the installation; T.Loop hosts the equipment.

The double stronghold is real in the standings. In the October 19 observations just before 6 pm Eastern, Tufa led ARC-AGI-2 and ARC-AGI-3, with Yi-Chia Chen second in each. The hardware announcement adds a striking new view of the lab behind those entries. It does not establish which machines produced the scores already on the board.

There is a callback for readers of our October 9 rabbit-and-spider report. Responding to a temporary setback, Tufa pledged to crush its competitors with “overwhelming resources and compute.” That was sporting bravado, accompanied by AI artwork. Ten days later, the lab has supplied a concrete hardware announcement to go alongside the rhetoric.

sections.heading: Inside each rack
sections.text:
NVIDIA’s published GB300 NVL72 configuration packs 72 Blackwell Ultra GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs into a liquid-cooled rack. Across Tufa’s two announced racks, that means 144 GPUs and 72 CPUs. Using NVIDIA’s reference specifications, the pair has about 40 TB of GPU memory plus 34 TB of CPU memory — roughly 74 TB combined.

Each rack provides up to 576 TB per second of aggregate GPU-memory bandwidth and 130 TB per second of NVLink bandwidth between its GPUs. The important distinction is where data moves: memory bandwidth feeds the processors; NVLink lets the GPUs exchange work inside the rack. Two racks do not automatically become one 144-GPU NVLink domain.

The advertised FP4 arithmetic ceiling is 1,080 petaflops per rack without sparsity, or 2,160 across two. NVIDIA also lists 1,440 per rack with sparsity. These are low-precision hardware ratings, not measured ARC speedups. They describe the standard platform; Tufa has not published a complete configuration or utilization report.

sections.heading: The deployment film, for readers short on time
sections.text:
DELTA’s October 19 YouTube film, Inside an NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 Deployment: TUFA Labs, follows the installation in Stockholm. The linked source below opens the full video. These are its essential moments.

At 1:26, founder Benjamin Crouzier introduces Tufa as an independent AI capability and safety research group. Around 4:17, he describes moving from DGX B200 systems to GB300 and a new workflow: faster work is the expectation, but he cautions against a direct comparison. At 7:50–8:10, he explains the ambition: run training rather than only download finished models, and investigate efficiency and alignment.

sections.heading: The unglamorous work behind the enormous machine
sections.text:
Around 2:04, the film reports that the equipment was connected within two days, following months of preparation. DELTA engineer Ramon Lenck describes planning power, cooling, networking and even cable lengths. At 3:31, the team explains the reinforced floor and plates used to spread the load.

Around 5:03, unpacking alone requires a large clear area and several people. At 6:21–6:52, the crew describes depressurizing and flushing the cooling circuits with hundreds of litres of coolant before final connections. The takeaway: this is a facility project, not merely two cabinets delivered to a server room.

sections.heading: What the challengers can read into it
sections.text:
Tufa’s announcement is evidence of greater research capacity. The two leading public entries make it consequential competition news. The next question is what Tufa builds and demonstrates with it. Neither the post nor the deployment film allocates a rack to each contest, discloses an ARC training recipe, or ties a particular submission to this installation.

The vast data-citadel interior is the sporting metaphor; the two racks are the hardware Tufa says is now live.

sections.heading: A new name near the gold line
sections.text:
wkdrbwnd1 reached 26th at 36.77 in the final observation before the Early cutoff. The recorded score transition was from 30.70, with the event showing a climb from 483rd. That leaves 1.21 points to the provisional public gold cutoff of 37.98. It is the morning’s sharpest late move near that boundary, without a change at the top.

goonew also made headway, adding 3.86 since the midnight comparison to reach 35.91 and close 38th. Its earlier score event put it 37th; the closing board moved it back one place. Those are two observations of the same advance, not two separate gains.

sections.text:
Tufa Labs leads at 68.91, with Yi-Chia Chen second at 67.49. Their gap remains 1.42 points. Team Turducken is third at 52.82, ahead of mtg and the last dance. NVARC3 remains tenth at 43.94. All ten leading entries retain their places and scores against the midnight comparison.

sections.heading: A fixed gold line, a moving field
sections.text:
The wire’s earlier report put _LT_zyc at 35th after a rise to 36.00. That rolling-window report supplies context for the chase; it is not a fresh gain to add to this issue’s midnight totals. The same distinction applies to the wire’s earlier fall in the gold line: the closing gold cutoff is still 37.98, matching the midnight baseline.

pensukesan’s later recorded transition lifted its score from 29.97 to 34.99; it closes 47th. There is activity beneath the leaders even while the leading ten hold. Public medal positions remain provisional.
